copy: Home › Grooming schedule

You’re working out a routine, not learning a technique. How often your dog needs each grooming job depends mostly on the coat, then on your dog’s lifestyle and condition. This page turns that into a schedule you can keep.
By Grooming Dogs · Updated October 5, 2026
This page covers how often . For how to , each task links to its own guide. Not sure what coat your dog has? Identify your dog’s coat type first.
Photo: Ron Lach / Pexels

Short answer: There’s no single schedule that suits every dog. How often to brush, bathe, trim nails, clean ears and brush teeth depends on your dog’s coat, the task itself, how your dog lives, and their health. Coat type makes the biggest difference to brushing, and to whether your dog needs regular professional grooming. Use the tables below as a starting point, then adjust for your dog.
Grooming needs vary by breed, coat type and lifestyle [2] . Brushing is where the coat makes the biggest difference.
Short, smooth coats need very little.
Long, silky and curly coats tangle and mat easily, so they need attention every day [1] [3] .
Coats that keep growing need regular haircuts, so they have professional grooming on a cycle.
Other jobs, such as nails, ears and teeth, depend less on the coat and more on the individual dog. They have their own table below.

Where these figures come from: These intervals come from published guidance by animal-welfare and dog organizations, listed under Sources. Where they differ, we show the range. They are starting points for a healthy adult dog, not rules. Your vet or groomer may advise differently for your dog.

How to do each task: bathing · brushing · nails · ears · teeth .
The tables describe a healthy adult dog. Adjust them for yours.
Puppies don’t need a full adult schedule yet. What matters more is getting them used to being handled and groomed, little and often. See grooming a puppy .
Older dogs often cope better with shorter, more frequent sessions than one long one. They may also need closer attention to nails. See grooming an older dog .
Dogs that spend a lot of time outdoors may need baths more often than the table suggests [1] . Muddy walks and swimming mean more frequent rinsing and drying, and more checks for tangles.

Some dogs with skin problems need a different bathing routine [1] , sometimes with medicated products. Follow your vet’s instructions rather than the table. Never treat a skin or ear problem by simply grooming more often. If you notice redness, sores, a bad smell, heavy scratching or painful mats, stop and ask your vet.
The calendar is a guide. These signs mean a job is due now, whatever the date:
Nails clicking on hard floors [2] , or nearly touching the ground as your dog walks [1] .
Tangles or knots forming, especially behind the ears, under the legs and around the collar. Brush before they become mats.
A dirty or smelly coat after outdoor activity.
Dirt or wax on the visible part of the ears.
Hair growing into the eyes or between the paw pads, on coats that keep growing.
If a sign looks more like a health problem than a grooming job, see problems after grooming or contact your vet. Examples: a red or painful ear, broken skin, or a sudden change in the coat.
How often depends on the coat:
Long-coated dogs: a professional groom (bath and haircut) every four to eight weeks is typical [1] [3] .
Curly coats: regular professional care. Your groomer will set the interval by how short the coat is kept [2] .
Short, smooth coats: these dogs generally need less extensive grooming [2] , and many never need a regular professional appointment.
Double and wiry coats: often managed at home, with a groomer for de-shedding or coat work when needed.
Daily or weekly brushing at home between appointments keeps a long coat manageable. It doesn’t replace the haircut, though.

Teeth: if daily isn’t realistic, a few times a week still helps [2] .

A practical tip: pair jobs with something you already do. For example, brush after the evening walk, and do nails and ears on the first weekend of the month. A routine you can keep is better than a perfect one you can’t.
Can I bathe my dog every week?

Many dogs need only occasional baths rather than frequent washing [2] . Unless your vet has recommended a bathing routine for a skin condition, the coat-type table is a better guide than a weekly habit. If your dog gets dirty, a rinse and a thorough dry is often enough.
Is it bad never to bathe my dog?

Yes. Even dogs that rarely get dirty benefit from a bath at least once every three months [1] . Dogs that spend a lot of time outdoors, or have skin problems, may need baths more often [1] . For skin problems, follow your vet’s advice.
How often should a short-haired dog be groomed?

Brush once a week [1] [3] . Bathe occasionally, roughly every month to every three months [1] [3] . Check nails and ears as in the table above. Short-haired dogs rarely need a regular professional groom [2] .
